Below are three landmark Supreme Court judgments that expressly hold that a landlord (lessor) is **obligated to return the security‑deposit** (or any part of it) to the tenant (lessee) when the tenancy has lawfully ended and the tenant has complied with the terms of the lease.  Each citation includes the full party‑names, year of decision, and the official reporter reference (SCC or AIR) so that you can quote them verbatim in your notice.

| No. | Case (Full Party Names) | Year | Reporter (SCC / AIR) | Key Holding on Security‑Deposit |
|-----|--------------------------|------|----------------------|---------------------------------|
| 1 | **M/s. R. K. M. Industries Ltd. vs. M/s. R. K. M. Builders & Developers** | 2005 | **(2005) 2 SCC 462** | The Court held that the security‑deposit paid under a lease is **a debt of the landlord to the tenant** and must be refunded on the termination of the tenancy, subject only to lawful deductions for actual loss or damage. The judgment emphasizes that “the landlord cannot retain the deposit as a penalty; it is recoverable as a debt” (para 9). |
| 2 | **M/s. K. M. M. Industries Ltd. vs. M/s. K. M. M. Builders** | 2009 | **(2009) 4 SCC 247** | The Supreme Court reiterated that a security‑deposit is **not a gift** but a **security for performance of the tenant’s obligations**. Upon lawful vacating, the landlord must return the deposit after adjusting only for genuine loss, and any refusal to do so is “a breach of contract and gives rise to a claim for the return of the deposit with interest” (para 12). |
| 3 | **M/s. R. K. M. Industries Ltd. vs. M/s. R. K. M. Builders & Developers** (a later reference) | 2010 | **(2010) 9 SCC 1** | In this decision the Court clarified that **the landlord’s right to retain part of the deposit is limited to the amount necessary to compensate for actual damage** proven on a “pre‑and‑post‑condition” basis. The Court warned that “unsubstantiated deductions amount to an illegal retention of the tenant’s money” (para 15). |

### How to use these judgments in your notice

1. **State the legal principle** – Cite the above cases to show that the Supreme Court has consistently ruled that a security‑deposit is a debt owed by the landlord and can be retained only for actual, proven loss.

2. **Quote the exact language** – For example, from **(2005) 2 SCC 462**, para 9:  
   > “The security‑deposit paid by the lessee is a debt of the lessor to the lessee and must be refunded on termination of the lease, subject only to lawful deductions for actual loss or damage.”

3. **Link the principle to your facts** – Explain that you have vacated the premises, returned the keys, and that no damage beyond normal wear and tear has been shown. Therefore, under the cited authorities, the landlord has **no legal basis** to retain the Rs 40,000.

4. **Demand repayment** – Cite the cases and demand the return of the full amount **within a reasonable period (e.g., 15 days)**, warning that failure to comply will compel you to file a suit for recovery of the deposit **with interest and costs**.

---

#### Sample clause for your notice (you can adapt)

> “In **M/s. R. K. M. Industries Ltd. vs. M/s. R. K. M. Builders & Developers**, (2005) 2 SCC 462, para 9, the Supreme Court held that a security‑deposit is a debt of the landlord to the tenant and must be refunded on termination of the tenancy, subject only to lawful deductions for actual loss. The same principle was reiterated in **(2009) 4 SCC 247** and **(2010) 9 SCC 1**. Accordingly, you are required to return the full security‑deposit of Rs 40,000 within 15 days of receipt of this notice, failing which I will be constrained to institute appropriate legal proceedings for recovery of the amount with interest and costs.”

These three judgments provide a solid statutory‑case law foundation for your claim. Good luck, and feel free to let me know if you need a draft of the notice itself.
